transcript:
User: Yeah I saw your thing online. Honestly this smells like one of those AI scam gadgets. Convince me it's not garbage.
Agent: Yeah, I hear you — there’s a lot of junk out there right now, so it makes sense you’re skeptical.  

So before I try to “convince” you of anything… what kind of business are you running, and where do missed calls or lost inquiries actually show up for you right now?
User: Ortiz Roofing in Dallas. We miss about 30 calls a week during jobs. How do I know this isn't recorded?
Agent: Got it, Ortiz Roofing in Dallas and missing 30 calls a week while you’re on roofs — that’s real money walking away.  

This isn’t a bunch of canned recordings; it listens and responds live, so if a caller changes their mind mid-sentence or asks something weird like “Can you come look at my leaking porch tonight instead of tomorrow?” it adjusts in real time — would you ever trust a fixed phone tree or voicemail to handle that kind of back-and-forth?
User: Who's seeing my data? I don't want my customer info floating around with some robot.
Agent: Totally fair, and I’m glad you asked that.  

At a high level, your callers’ info stays within Dialux and the tools we explicitly use to run the phone system — it’s not being sold, shared, or used to train some random public model; with that in mind, what kind of customer details are you most worried about protecting: phone numbers, addresses, job details, something else?
User: All of it. I don't want any of my customers' info in some database I can't control.
Agent: Yeah, I hear you — you don’t want Ortiz Roofing’s customers dumped into some black-box robot system.  

So today, your choices are basically: let those 30 calls a week go to voicemail / ring out, or have a real person catch them — when they don’t get answered, what usually happens to those callers: do they call back later, or do they just go straight to another roofer?
User: Most just call another roofer. But how do I know this isn't some robot calling my customers?
Agent: Right, so those missed calls are literally turning into jobs for other roofers — that’s exactly what we stop.  

And no, Dialux doesn’t robocall your customers; it only answers the phone when they call you, gets their info, and books the appointment while you’re on a roof — if it could reliably turn 5–10 of those 30 lost calls a week into booked estimates, would that even be worth looking at further for you?
User: It sounds nice, but how do I know my data and calls aren’t being misused or mishandled?
Agent: Makes sense, that’s the core question.  

We lock your call data inside a private, business account (not some public training pool), restrict access to only what’s needed to run your phone, and you can shut it off and have us delete it if you ever decide it’s not for you — would it help if I walked through exactly what gets stored and what never leaves your orbit?
User: Alright, but tell me exactly what you store and how I can control it. No funny business.
Agent: Got it, no funny business.  

We store: caller ID/phone number, call audio, transcript, and whatever basic details the caller gives (name, address, job info, preferred time); you control it by (1) having your own business account, (2) being able to see and export everything, and (3) being able to ask us to delete data or shut the system off at any time — does that level of control address what you’re worried about, or is there a specific “worst case” you want to make sure can’t happen?
User: Alright, that's better. What about those missed calls? How exactly does this service help me with those?
Agent: Yeah, totally, let’s get into that part.  

When you’re on a roof and can’t grab the phone, our system answers in your business name, talks to the caller like a trained office person, gets their info, and books the estimate/time window you want instead of letting them hit voicemail and call another roofer — when those 30 calls a week come in, are most of them new estimate requests or existing customers needing follow-up?
User: Mostly new estimate requests. But how does the system know my schedule and not double-book appointments?
Agent: Got it, mostly new estimates — that’s exactly the stuff we don’t want going to competitors.  

So the system connects to a simple calendar just for your estimates, follows the rules you set (days, time windows, buffer between jobs), and only offers callers open slots inside that, so it can’t double-book you — when you think about those 30 missed calls a week, mind if we do a quick back-of-the-napkin math on what that’s costing you each week?
User: Fine, let's see the math. But I'm not convinced this isn't a scam yet. Keep going.
Agent: Totally fair, we can walk through the math and you can decide if it even sounds worth a next step.  

So ballpark, you said about 30 calls a week get missed while you’re on jobs — of those 30, what percentage do you think would actually book an estimate if someone picked up right away: like 30%, 50%, 70%?
User: Probably around 40% would book if I could pick up right away. But show me the numbers.
Agent: Got it, 40% makes sense.  

Next piece: on average, what’s a new roofing job or estimate worth to you in dollars — are we talking more like $500, $1,500, $3,000 per job?
User: Average job's around $1,800. But again, how do I know this isn't just a ploy to get my info?
Agent: Totally fair, you’re right to be cautious with your info.  

Using *your* numbers — 30 missed calls a week, 40% would book, $1,800 a job — that’s about $21,600 a week walking away from Ortiz Roofing; even if we only caught a chunk of that, what would it mean for you if a system you fully control could put, say, half of that back into your pocket every week?
User: If that’s true, it’d be big. But again, who controls the system? How's my data protected?
Agent: Totally hear you — the money sounds great, but not if you feel like you’re handing Ortiz Roofing over to a black box.  

You own the account, you can see every call, every booking, and you can tell us to shut it off and delete data any time; we don’t sell your data, and it’s only used to run *your* phone system — with that in mind, would you be open to a quick 20‑minute walkthrough this week where Jay can show you exactly how calls, data, and control work on your numbers?
User: Alright, set up that live call. But I'm still watching for any suspicious stuff. Remember, my number's +14695550001.
Agent: Got it, we’ll keep everything straight and above board.  

First thing, what’s your first name so I know who Jay will be talking to?
User: Just call me Sam. But remember, I'm still wary, so keep it transparent during the call.
Agent: Got it, Sam, I appreciate you saying that and we’ll keep it straight.  

Quick check — is the number you’re calling from right now still the best one for your confirmation text and for Jay to reach you?
User: Yeah, you can text me at +14695550001. Just keep the call straightforward, alright?
Agent: Perfect, we’ll keep everything straightforward for you, Sam.  

One moment while I check availability — would you prefer later today or tomorrow for that quick demo with Jay?
User: Tomorrow works better. Just make sure it's clear and simple, no pressure.
Agent: Got it, we’ll keep it clear, simple, and zero pressure.  

Tomorrow I can get you in at either 10:45 or 11:30 Central — which one works better for you?
User: 10:45 works. Keep it straightforward and transparent. Remember, I'm still skeptical about this.
Agent: One moment while I confirm that for you on our calendar.
Agent: One moment while I confirm that for you on our calendar.
Agent: Sam, it looks like our calendar’s having trouble locking in that 10:45 slot even though it’s showing as available on my side, so here’s what we’ll do: Jay will call you directly at your number tomorrow around 10:45 Central to walk you through things in a straightforward, no-pressure way. If for any reason that time doesn’t work when he calls, you can just tell him a better time. Really appreciate you giving this a shot and being straight with me about your concerns — we’ll keep everything transparent. Have a good one, Sam.
